chunks: Why boosts are less efficient than bucks. The question: Why are they less efficient than buck converters?
Boosts often lose more power than bucks, for two reasons. The inductor and switch carry more current than the load does, since the input current is I out over (1-D) .
And in a simple boost, the diode carries all of the output current all of the time, wasting power in its forward drop.
The gap is not fundamental: a synchronous boost with similar parts gets close to a buck.
Picture a toll booth. In a buck, the cars pay the toll only part of the time.
In a simple boost, every car that reaches the output has to pay the toll, which is the diode's forward voltage. So the toll collected over a day is larger.
If you replace the toll booth with an open lane (a synchronous switch), the extra cost almost disappears.
With a diode the efficiency is lower at small boost ratios, because V F equals 0.

"Two things: current and the diode.
In a boost the inductor and switch carry I out over (1-D) , more than the load current, and conduction loss goes with current squared, so DCR and R DS(on) losses are bigger.
In a non-synchronous boost the diode also carries the full load current at V F , which is about 8% of a 5 volts, 1 amps output.
Add pulsed output current, higher switch-node voltage and duty-cycle limits. With synchronous rectification and a modest ratio the gap mostly closes."
